toc.title: Coping, unhealthy coping, and behavioral adaptations
Two paths from the same intersection
How behavioral adaptations crowd out helpful thoughts

blocks.p: Is binge eating a behavioral adaptation, or something else? Let's look at it through the Polyvagal Theory, and along the way, at behavioral adaptations in general.

A behavioral adaptation is something we do to reduce the intensity of defensive activation. It makes what we feel inside more tolerable, or numbs it, or just reduces it. Teeth grinding, fidgeting, bullying, addictions. Binge eating could be one. So could hair pulling, drug use, or numbing out on your phone. All of these behaviors, and a whole bunch more, come from a dysregulated defensive autonomic state, like a rageful freeze or anxious flight activation.
Say you're coming out of shutdown and there's some returning sympathetic energy, some flight or fight energy. If that's too much for somebody, they might turn to binge eating as a way to reduce it.

blocks.h: Coping, unhealthy coping, and behavioral adaptations

blocks.p: A behavioral adaptation is not coping, exactly. Coping is getting through the moment. With a behavioral adaptation, you're not allowing the activation whatsoever. You're doing something to stop it.

Coping might be using a coloring book. You're not really grounding in safety, but you're distracting yourself. Coping might be playing a game on your phone, or checking out for a couple of hours to watch a movie.

A behavioral adaptation is unhealthy coping: distraction and numbing out. You're doing something that may even be counterproductive, something that's going to result in self-shame and blame. It's like you're reinforcing the very thing you're trying to get away from.

blocks.h: Two paths from the same intersection

blocks.p: Picture a road that comes up to an intersection with a stop sign. That spot right before the stop sign is defensive activation. Maybe you're coming out of shutdown into flight or fight activation, or freeze is attempting to discharge its flight or fight energy. At that point, a couple of things could happen.

Path B is the behavioral adaptation. The defensive state reactivates at the stop sign, and you turn to binge eating. It kind of feels better. It kind of feels like you're moving toward self-regulation, because you feel less defensive activation. But it takes you right back to the starting point. It's pseudo self-regulatory. It's kind of like coping, but you end up right back where you were.

As you spiral back, there are thoughts of self-blame, judgment, and shame: "How could I do this? I knew it. I'm worthless." Behavioral adaptations come along with those negative cognitions, and with feelings of shame, embarrassment, and humiliation. There's no mindfulness on path B. It's very reactive. You're just trying to get rid of the feelings.
Path B goes in a circle. It sets you right back up for the exact same situation, over and over. It feels good, and then you crash. It's very much like an addiction, I would say.

Path A is self-regulation. Here you listen to your body's needs. You notice that flight or fight activation coming back into your system, and you allow it through the AWE method: allow, witness, experience. Then you may notice an impulse underneath the returning sympathetic energy. If you notice some returning anger, power, or fight energy, maybe the impulse is to squeeze or to push. If you follow that impulse, it leads you up the self-regulation path.

On path A, there's no judgment. There's curiosity and interest, and from that curiosity, you're able to let the impulse climb your polyvagal ladder, using those often very hidden impulses that underlie our emotions and our cognitions.
So path B mimics path A, but it takes you right back.

Would OCD be something like a behavioral adaptation? I think so. I think it comes specifically from a very panicky, flight-flavored freeze. Mild anxiety is different. There are ways to cope with anxiety, but that's not OCD. I would argue OCD comes from a really intense, panic-flavored freeze state. Maybe rage or fight flavored too, but definitely panic.
So say you're going up that path and the intense freeze panic energy hits, and the brain says, "I need to do something to make this feel better." That's where the OCD thoughts come in.

One of my clients used really intensive prayer. She recognized it wasn't peaceful praying and connection. It was, "I have to do this to make myself feel better." She'd feel the activation, and her brain would go to all sorts of catastrophic thinking, like the death of her loved ones, or her mom abandoning her. Then her brain's solution would be: pray, pray, pray, pray. But it wasn't a calm, meditative, connective experience. It was intense, and she had to. It kind of made her feel better, but then the compulsion would come right back, along with the stuck state.

blocks.h: How behavioral adaptations crowd out helpful thoughts

blocks.p: Could a behavioral adaptation get in the way of more helpful cognitions? I think so. If you can actually feel what's happening within you, there will be cognitions about what to do with it, more compassionate ones.

If you can allow your defensive activation, your brain might come up with, "Hey, this would be a really good idea right now." If someone feels fight energy, their brain might say, "Now's a really good time to do some pushups," or "go for a swim," or "push against the wall," or maybe "just get a hug."

But if you go straight back to the behavioral adaptation, those cognitions won't come into your brain. Instead it's going to be, "I need a drink to make myself feel better." If that cognition is followed and acted on, the other, more helpful ones probably won't pop into your mind, or if they do, they won't be acted on.

One member described their own loop like this: on path A, you might feel an impulse to push something or pull something, to mobilize it, but a thought comes in that says, "Oh, you can't act out." So they act in instead.

I use that same idea in my book Trauma & the Polyvagal Paradigm. I call them cognitive adaptations: the brain comes up with a life theme to contain what's happening within us. "I can't act out. I can't make a scene." That cognition pops in and shuts down what may be rightful defensive activation.
